claim: Gait is impaired in musculoskeletal conditions, such as knee arthropathy.
source: Gait is impaired in musculoskeletal conditions, such as knee arthropathy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Gait analysis is used in clinical practice to inform diagnosis and monitor disease progression or intervention response.
source: Gait analysis is used in clinical practice to inform diagnosis and monitor disease progression or intervention response.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical practice without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: Clinical gait analysis relies on subjective visual observation of walking.
source: However, clinical gait analysis relies on subjective visual observation of walking as objective gait analysis has not been possible within clinical settings due to the expensive equipment, large-scale facilities, and highly trained staff required.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of current clinical practice.

claim: Objective gait analysis has not been possible within clinical settings due to the expensive equipment, large-scale facilities, and highly trained staff required.
source: However, clinical gait analysis relies on subjective visual observation of walking as objective gait analysis has not been possible within clinical settings due to the expensive equipment, large-scale facilities, and highly trained staff required.
evidence: This is stated as a known barrier to objective gait analysis in clinical settings.

claim: A machine learning model trained on force plate data collected in participants with knee arthropathy and controls was highly predictive of force plate data from a validation set (auROC = 0.86; auPR = 0.90).
source: To achieve this, we constructed a machine learning model, trained on force plate data collected in participants with knee arthropathy and controls. This model was highly predictive of force plate data from a validation set (area under the receiver operating characteristics curve [auROC] = 0.86; area under the precision-recall curve [auPR] = 0.90)
evidence: The abstract reports specific performance metrics (auROC and auPR) for the model on validation data.

claim: A machine learning model trained on force plate data was highly predictive of a separate, independent digital insole dataset containing control and knee osteoarthritis subjects (auROC = 0.83; auPR = 0.86).
source: This model was highly predictive of force plate data from a validation set (area under the receiver operating characteristics curve [auROC] = 0.86; area under the precision-recall curve [auPR] = 0.90) and of a separate, independent digital insole dataset containing control and knee osteoarthritis subjects (auROC = 0.83; auPR = 0.86).
evidence: The abstract reports specific performance metrics for the model on an independent digital insole dataset.

claim: A single stride of raw sensor time-series data could be accurately assigned to each subject.
source: After showing that digital insole-derived gait characteristics are comparable to traditional gait measurements, we next showed that a single stride of raw sensor time-series data could be accurately assigned to each subject, highlighting that individuals using digital insoles can be identified by their gait characteristics.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on analysis described in the manuscript.

claim: Individuals using digital insoles can be identified by their gait characteristics.
source: After showing that digital insole-derived gait characteristics are comparable to traditional gait measurements, we next showed that a single stride of raw sensor time-series data could be accurately assigned to each subject, highlighting that individuals using digital insoles can be identified by their gait characteristics.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the data analysis showing individual stride assignment.

claim: Gait assessment plays several roles in clinical practice and research for many musculoskeletal and orthopedic diseases, such as diagnosis, guiding treatment selection, and measuring intervention response.
source: Gait assessment plays several roles in clinical practice and research for many musculoskeletal and orthopedic diseases, such as diagnosis, guiding treatment selection, and measuring intervention response. (Lord et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lord et al., 1998.

claim: Knee osteoarthritis contributes to altered gait as individuals try to avoid knee pain and cartilage contact stress.
source: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) contributes to altered gait as individuals try to avoid knee pain and cartilage contact stress (i.e., weight shift or joint loading onto the non-affected limb) (Iijima et al., 2019; Kaufman et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Iijima et al., 2019 and Kaufman et al., 2001.

claim: Those with knee OA commonly have increased lateral trunk lean toward the ipsilateral limb, along with non-significantly increased trunk/pelvic flexion and resultant significant alterations in external hip adduction moments.
source: Those with knee OA commonly have increased lateral trunk lean toward the ipsilateral limb, along with non-significantly increased trunk/pelvic flexion and resultant significant alterations in external hip adduction moments (Iijima et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iijima et al., 2019.

claim: Clinically, gait is examined in knee OA through clinical visual observation of walking, which is subjective and dependent on expertise.
source: Clinically, gait is examined in knee OA through clinical visual observation of walking, which is subjective and dependent on expertise.
evidence: This is stated as a description of current clinical practice.

claim: Gait has been traditionally objectively assessed in specialized gait laboratories with expensive equipment, such as force platforms, with or without a motion-tracking system.
source: Beyond visual observation, gait has been traditionally objectively assessed in specialized gait laboratories with expensive equipment, such as force platforms, with or without a motion-tracking system.
evidence: This is stated as established practice in gait analysis.

claim: Gait laboratories are generally not available or feasible within clinical settings due to cost, need for highly trained staff to operate equipment, and the size of equipment.
source: However, gait laboratories are generally not available or feasible within clinical settings due to cost, need for highly trained staff to operate equipment, and the size of equipment.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of gait laboratory use in clinical settings.

claim: Wearable sensors offer an alternative approach to assessment of gait in those with knee OA.
source: Wearable sensors offer an alternative approach to assessment of gait in those with knee OA (Mills et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mills et al., 2013.

claim: Wearable sensors can be deployed within any environment or setting.
source: Wearable sensors offer an alternative approach to assessment of gait in those with knee OA (Mills et al., 2013) as they can be deployed within any environment or setting (Stern et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2022.

claim: Wearable sensors are relatively low-cost.
source: Wearable sensors offer an alternative approach to assessment of gait in those with knee OA (Mills et al., 2013) as they can be deployed within any environment or setting (Stern et al., 2022), are relatively low-cost, and can provide outcomes automatically without the need for highly experienced or trained staff.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of wearable sensors.

claim: Wearable sensors can provide outcomes automatically without the need for highly experienced or trained staff.
source: Wearable sensors offer an alternative approach to assessment of gait in those with knee OA (Mills et al., 2013) as they can be deployed within any environment or setting (Stern et al., 2022), are relatively low-cost, and can provide outcomes automatically without the need for highly experienced or trained staff.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of wearable sensors.

claim: Vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) is a gait characteristic that is impaired within knee OA as it relates to the bilateral weightbearing capabilities of the patient.
source: Vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) is a gait characteristic that is impaired within knee OA as it relates to the bilateral weightbearing capabilities of the patient (i.e., greater peak vGRF) (Creaby et al., 2013; Davis et al., 2019; Trentadue et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Creaby et al., 2013; Davis et al., 2019; Trentadue et al., 2021.

claim: Traditionally, vGRF is objectively examined using force plates, which can provide three components of force (vertical, anterior-posterior, and medio-lateral).
source: Traditionally, vGRF is objectively examined using force plates, which can provide three components of force (vertical, anterior-posterior, and medio-lateral) (Creaby et al., 2013; Davis et al., 2019; Trentadue et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Creaby et al., 2013; Davis et al., 2019; Trentadue et al., 2021.

claim: Force plate signals can provide information on gait characteristics, postural stability, as well as direction, strength, and duration of stance phase.
source: Force plate signals can provide information on gait characteristics, postural stability, as well as direction, strength, and duration of stance phase (Arslan et al., 2019; Whittle, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Arslan et al., 2019 and Whittle, 2007.

claim: Force plates only capture intermittent data on vGRF (single or several steps) within controlled experiments that do not represent real-world overground walking.
source: However, force plates only capture intermittent data on vGRF (single or several steps) within controlled experiments that do not represent real-world overground walking.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of force plate technology.

claim: Technological development has led to digital insoles (wearables) that can capture vGRF and other gait characteristics that are relevant to knee OA assessment.
source: Technological development has led to digital insoles (wearables) that can capture vGRF and other gait characteristics that are relevant to knee OA assessment, which could be used within free-living environments (Stern et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2022.

claim: Digital insoles could be used within free-living environments.
source: Technological development has led to digital insoles (wearables) that can capture vGRF and other gait characteristics that are relevant to knee OA assessment, which could be used within free-living environments (Stern et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stern et al., 2022.

claim: Clinical application of wearable digital insoles for gait analysis in knee OA is limited by a paucity of analytical validation data.
source: However, clinical application of wearable digital insoles for gait analysis in knee OA is limited by a paucity of analytical validation data (including face, criterion, and construct validity), such as comparison of gait outcome measures in those with knee OA to 'gold-standard' laboratory references (e.g., force plate outcomes) (Goldsack et al., 2020; Rochester et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldsack et al., 2020 and Rochester et al., 2020.

claim: Gait quantitation generates dense raw sensor time-series data with nonlinear relationships that make analysis and interpretation challenging.
source: Gait quantitation generates dense raw sensor time-series data with nonlinear relationships that make analysis and interpretation challenging.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of gait data.

claim: Digital gait data analysis pipelines suffer from a lack of well-established analytical methods compared to other biomarker data types.
source: As a class, digital gait data analysis pipelines suffer from a lack of well-established analytical methods compared to other biomarker data types (Wipperman et al., 2022; Crouthamel et al., 2021; Horst et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wipperman et al., 2022; Crouthamel et al., 2021; Horst et al., 2019.

claim: There is interest in developing more streamlined ('light-weight') gait algorithms and data processing pipelines using machine learning to automate and process large volumes of novel digital data obtained from wearable devices.
source: Recently, there is interest in developing more streamlined ('light-weight') gait algorithms and data processing pipelines using machine learning (ML) to automate and process large volumes of novel digital data obtained from wearable devices (Celik et al., 2022; Godfrey et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Celik et al., 2022 and Godfrey et al., 2018.

claim: Selection of the appropriate modeling modalities for a particular clinical question is challenging.
source: Selection of the appropriate modeling modalities for a particular clinical question is challenging (Horst et al., 2019; Slijepcevic et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horst et al., 2019 and Slijepcevic et al., 2022.

claim: Deep learning models are better suited to handle high-throughput, multimodal data streams, such as raw sensor time series.
source: For example, deep learning models are better suited to handle high-throughput, multimodal data streams, such as raw sensor time series (Alias, 2018; Briouza et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alias, 2018 and Briouza et al., 2021.

claim: Deep learning models typically require larger datasets than classical statistical or ML methods (in terms of both features and sample size).
source: For example, deep learning models are better suited to handle high-throughput, multimodal data streams, such as raw sensor time series (Alias, 2018; Briouza et al., 2021), but typically require larger datasets than classical statistical or ML methods (in terms of both features and sample size).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of deep learning models.

claim: The GaitRec Force Plate study included subjects with knee injuries (N = 625) and controls (N = 211).
source: We obtained vGRF data from the three studies: the GaitRec Force Plate study of subjects with knee injuries (N = 625) and controls (N = 211)
evidence: This describes the composition of one of the datasets used in the study.

claim: Two digital insole studies included controls (N = 22) and subjects with knee OA (N = 40).
source: We obtained vGRF data from the three studies: the GaitRec Force Plate study of subjects with knee injuries (N = 625) and controls (N = 211) and two digital insole studies in controls (N = 22) and subjects with knee OA (N = 40), respectively (Figure 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the composition of the digital insole datasets used in the study.

claim: The means of vGRF curves within each disease category are similar across platforms (force plate and digital insole).
source: We plotted raw and normalized vGRF values recorded by force plate and digital insole devices and observed by visual inspection that the means of vGRF curves within each disease category are similar across platforms (Figure 2A), which highlights face validity of the digital insoles (i.e., the insole data appeared similar to the force plate data).
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The similarity of vGRF curves across platforms highlights face validity of the digital insoles.
source: We plotted raw and normalized vGRF values recorded by force plate and digital insole devices and observed by visual inspection that the means of vGRF curves within each disease category are similar across platforms (Figure 2A), which highlights face validity of the digital insoles (i.e., the insole data appeared similar to the force plate data).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the similarity observed in Figure 2A.

claim: Individuals with knee arthropathy from all evaluated datasets displayed a qualitatively different gait signature than controls, with a 'flatter' vGRF curve shape during the middle of stance phase.
source: Specifically, individuals with knee arthropathy from all evaluated datasets displayed a qualitatively different gait signature than controls, with a 'flatter' vGRF curve shape during the middle of stance phase (we use the term 'arthropathy' to encompass both knee injury and OA).
evidence: This is based on observation of the vGRF data patterns described in the text and shown in figures.

claim: Using UMAP dimension reduction, subjects at a population level separated out by arthropathy status (knee arthropathies vs controls) rather than by measurement platform.
source: Using a dimension reduction approach Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) with normalized vGRF data from each subject in two dimensions, subjects at a population level separated out by arthropathy status (knee arthropathies vs controls) rather than by measurement platform (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on UMAP analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The arthropathy state is the major contributor to the vGRF signal for most of the vGRF curve.
source: We observed that the disease state is the major contributor to vGRF for most of the curve, with age, sex, and body weight also explaining a smaller proportion of the variance.
evidence: This is based on linear modeling analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Age, sex, and body weight explain a smaller proportion of the variance in vGRF compared to disease state.
source: We observed that the disease state is the major contributor to vGRF for most of the curve, with age, sex, and body weight also explaining a smaller proportion of the variance.
evidence: This is based on linear modeling analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SVM model indicated strong predictive power to classify control versus knee injury subjects using force plate data when evaluated using fivefold cross-validation (left knee: auROC = 0.92 [SD = 0.03], auPR = 0.94 [SD = 0.03]; right knee: auROC = 0.94 [SD = 0.02], auPR = 0.96 [SD = 0.01]).
source: The model indicated strong predictive power to classify control versus knee injury subjects using force plate data when evaluated using fivefold cross-validation of the training/validation dataset, a standard method of assessing model performance (left knee: area under the receiver operating characteristics curve [auROC] = 0.92 [SD = 0.03], area under the precision-recall curve [auPR] = 0.94 [SD = 0.03]; right knee: auROC = 0.94 [SD = 0.02], auPR = 0.96 [SD = 0.01]).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics from the cross-validation analysis.

claim: The predictive power of the SVM model was strong when assessed on the hold-out test dataset (left knee: auROC = 0.95, auPR = 0.95; right knee: auROC = 0.93, auPR = 0.95).
source: The predictive power was also strong when assessed on the hold-out test dataset, which was not used for training of the SVM model (left knee: auROC = 0.95, auPR = 0.95; right knee: auROC = 0.93, auPR = 0.95) (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics from the hold-out test set analysis.

claim: For the digital insole, an SVM model trained only on force plate data performed as well on the digital insole data (left knee: auROC = 0.93, auPR = 0.94; right knee: auROC = 0.93, auPR = 0.94) as it did on the hold-out force plate test data.
source: We found that for the digital insole an SVM model trained only on force plate data performed as well on the digital insole data (left knee: auROC = 0.93, auPR = 0.94; right knee: auROC = 0.93, auPR = 0.94) as it did on the hold-out force plate test data (Figure 2E and E; Table 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics comparing digital insole and force plate test data.

claim: Walking speed alone was able to discriminate between knee OA subjects and controls (auROC = 0.981, auPR = 0.983).
source: We found that walking speed alone was able to discriminate between knee OA subjects and controls (auROC = 0.981, auPR = 0.983).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics for walking speed as a predictor.

claim: vGRF with the digital insole demonstrated high predictive power (LOOCV: auROC = 0.984, auPR = 0.990; r5FCV: auROC = 0.988, auPR = 0.992).
source: vGRF with the digital insole also demonstrated high predictive power (LOOCV: auROC = 0.984, auPR = 0.990; r5FCV: auROC = 0.988, auPR = 0.992).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics for vGRF-based classification.

claim: Using derived gait characteristics that excluded the 14 characteristics strongly correlated to walking speed, classification accuracy was high (LOOCV: auROC = 0.997, auPR = 0.988; r5FCV: auROC = 0.996, auPR = 0.986).
source: Using derived gait characteristics that excluded the 14 characteristics strongly correlated to walking speed, we found even better classification accuracy (LOOCV: auROC = 0.997, auPR = 0.988; r5FCV: auROC = 0.996, auPR = 0.986).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics for derived gait characteristics excluding speed-correlated features.

claim: The most important discriminating parameters included takeoff dynamics, max force (N), mean COP velocity (mm/s), and gait line-associated parameters (sd x and sd y of gait line start point [mm]).
source: The most important discriminating parameters included takeoff dynamics, max force (N), mean COP velocity (mm/s), and gait line-associated parameters (sd x and sd y of gait line start point [mm]) (Supplementary file 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of feature importance in the model.

claim: Flattened strides from raw sensor data were predictive (LOOCV: auROC = 0.997, auPR = 0.998).
source: Flattened strides from raw sensor data, which is also independent of walking speed as each stride was interpolated to a consistent 100 timepoints, also were predictive (LOOCV: auROC = 0.997, auPR = 0.998) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports specific performance metrics for raw sensor data analysis.

claim: Classification accuracy for control versus knee OA depends on the type of sensor, the timepoint along a stride, and the foot (left vs right).
source: We trained additional SVM models on subsets of sensor type at each timepoint (Figure 4F) and found that classification accuracy for control versus knee OA depends on the type of sensor, the timepoint along a stride, and the foot (left vs right).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sensor-specific and timepoint-specific classification accuracy shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Measurements of pressure and force from a foot had greater mean classification accuracy during the stance phase of that foot.
source: Measurements of pressure and force from a foot had greater mean classification accuracy during the stance phase of that foot.
evidence: This is based on analysis of sensor-specific classification accuracy.

claim: The CNN latent representation was best at minimizing distances of strides from the same subjects while maximizing the distances of strides from different subjects from the same class, as measured by Cohen's d effect size.
source: The CNN latent representation was best at minimizing distances of strides from the same subjects while maximizing the distances of strides from different subjects from the same class, as measured by Cohen's d effect size, suggesting that the CNN latent representations best capture gait individuality, and as such was used for follow-up analysis.
evidence: This is based on comparison of different representations using Cohen's d effect size.

claim: Within the training set, the consistency model produced lower distances than the individuality model in comparing strides within self from different days (p<0.001, paired t-test).
source: Within the training set, the consistency model, which was trained on both day 1 and 85 strides, produced lower distances than the individuality model, which was trained on only day 1 strides, in comparing strides within self from different days (p<0.001, paired t-test) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison between models with a specific p-value.

claim: Within the testing set, the consistency model produced lower distances than the individuality model in comparing strides within self from different days (nominal p=0.033, paired t-test).
source: Importantly, within the testing set, the consistency model produced lower distances than the individuality model in comparing strides within self from different days (nominal p=0.033, paired t-test)
evidence: This reports a statistical comparison between models with a specific p-value.

claim: Training across multiple days improves the ability of the CNN consistency model to identify features that remain consistent across multiple visits.
source: Importantly, within the testing set, the consistency model produced lower distances than the individuality model in comparing strides within self from different days (nominal p=0.033, paired t-test), suggesting that training across multiple days improves the ability of the CNN consistency model to identify features that remain consistent across multiple visits.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical comparison results.

claim: In the consistency model, the distances of the data to oneself were lower amongst strides from the same day versus different day in both training and testing participants (nominal p<0.001 and nominal p=0.004, respectively, t-test).
source: The results also show additional capacity for model improvement with respect to consistency of gait, as in the consistency model, the distances of the data to oneself were lower amongst strides from the same day versus different day in both training and testing participants (nominal p<0.001 and nominal p=0.004, respectively, t-test).
evidence: This reports statistical comparisons with specific p-values.

claim: The digital insoles appeared to have face (analytical) validity for vGRF measurement in knee OA and controls.
source: Overall, the digital insoles appeared to have face (analytical) validity for vGRF measurement in knee OA and controls (qualitatively appears to provide similar results to force plate data)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparison of digital insole and force plate data.

claim: Various insole-derived gait outcomes demonstrated early clinical validity as they provided clinically meaningful outcome measures for knee OA.
source: Overall, the digital insoles appeared to have face (analytical) validity for vGRF measurement in knee OA and controls (qualitatively appears to provide similar results to force plate data), and various insole-derived gait outcomes demonstrated early clinical validity as they provided clinically meaningful outcome measures for knee OA.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the ability of insole-derived outcomes to detect disease-specific patterns.

claim: The predictive performance of the ML model on data collected from a different device at different physical locations and experimental conditions suggests that the model was robust and generalizable (not overfit).
source: The predictive performance of the ML model on data collected from a different device at different physical locations and experimental conditions suggests that the model was robust and generalizable (not overfit).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's performance across different datasets and conditions.

claim: Disease status is the major signal observed in the vGRF data.
source: While our analysis may be confounded by variables like age, our results imply that disease status is the major signal we observe.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the linear modeling analysis showing disease as the major contributor to variance.

claim: vGRF data likely reflect true differences between control and knee arthropathy subjects.
source: Our results suggest that vGRF data likely reflect true differences between control and knee arthropathy subjects, suggesting that digital insoles may be used to screen for knee arthropathy and potentially other diseases that impact gait.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results showing consistent disease-related patterns in vGRF data.

claim: Digital insoles may be used to screen for knee arthropathy and potentially other diseases that impact gait.
source: Our results suggest that vGRF data likely reflect true differences between control and knee arthropathy subjects, suggesting that digital insoles may be used to screen for knee arthropathy and potentially other diseases that impact gait.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Speed-independent gait characteristics play an important role in identifying patients with knee arthropathy and controls.
source: Findings confirmed that speed-independent gait characteristics play an important role in identifying patients with knee arthropathy and controls.
evidence: This is based on the analysis showing high classification accuracy even when speed-correlated features were removed.

claim: Walking speed is a prognostic biomarker for mortality and a clinically meaningful outcome measure.
source: Despite walking speed being a prognostic biomarker for mortality and a clinically meaningful outcome measure, it lacks the ability to detect disease-specific impairments or potential improvements with intervention (i.e., speed is the accumulation of other gait characteristics, and more specific gait characteristics can be mapped to specific underlying musculoskeletal, neurological, or cardio-pulmonary impairment) (Morris et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morris et al., 2016 and Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: Walking speed lacks the ability to detect disease-specific impairments or potential improvements with intervention.
source: Despite walking speed being a prognostic biomarker for mortality and a clinically meaningful outcome measure, it lacks the ability to detect disease-specific impairments or potential improvements with intervention (i.e., speed is the accumulation of other gait characteristics, and more specific gait characteristics can be mapped to specific underlying musculoskeletal, neurological, or cardio-pulmonary impairment) (Morris et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morris et al., 2016 and Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: In addition to alterations in speed there are additional gait characteristics in knee OA that differentiate them from controls.
source: This highlights that in addition to alterations in speed there are additional gait characteristics in knee OA that differentiate them from controls.
evidence: This is based on the finding that speed-independent gait characteristics can classify knee OA versus controls.

claim: A strength of using digital insoles over other lower cost technology (e.g., Inertial Measurement Units, or IMUs) is that they can accurately capture the gait cycle and weight transfer/bearing in OA patients.
source: A strength of using digital insoles over other lower cost technology (e.g., Inertial Measurement Units, or IMUs) is that they can accurately capture the gait cycle and weight transfer/bearing in OA patients, which was our primary clinical focus here.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of digital insoles based on their measurement capabilities.

claim: Unlike IMUs that require algorithms to estimate the initial and final contact of the foot, digital insoles provide additional information such as the ability to determine when the foot is actually on the ground via raw pressure sensor data.
source: Unlike IMUs that require algorithms to estimate the initial and final contact of the foot (Paraschiv-Ionescu et al., 2020), digital insoles provide additional information such as the ability to determine when the foot is actually on the ground via raw pressure sensor data, thereby improving the accuracy of gait event detection and proceeding outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Paraschiv-Ionescu et al., 2020.

claim: Digital insoles are often used for analytical validation of IMU algorithms in clinical populations.
source: This is the reason why digital insoles are often used for analytical validation of IMU algorithms in clinical populations (Mazzà et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mazzà et al., 2021.

claim: Digital insoles may not be as hardwearing as IMUs (i.e., capacitors may deteriorate over time, so are not recommended for free-living assessment).
source: Although digital insoles may not be as hardwearing as IMUs (i.e., capacitors may deteriorate over time, so are not recommended for free-living assessment) (Vu et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vu et al., 2020.

claim: Digital insoles are useful clinical tools for active mobility tasks in an OA population as they provide gait- and pressure-related metrics that are relevant for this clinical condition.
source: Although digital insoles may not be as hardwearing as IMUs (i.e., capacitors may deteriorate over time, so are not recommended for free-living assessment) (Vu et al., 2020), they are useful clinical tools for active mobility tasks in an OA population as they provide gait- and pressure-related metrics that are relevant for this clinical condition.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of digital insoles for specific clinical applications.

claim: In free living settings, digital insoles may have issues with device placement and sensor deterioration.
source: Alternatively, in free living settings (e.g., passive monitoring with wearables over hours/days/weeks), digital insoles may have issues with device placement and sensor deterioration (Vu et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vu et al., 2020.

claim: IMUs have been shown to be comfortable and have high acceptance across various clinical populations.
source: Alternatively, in free living settings (e.g., passive monitoring with wearables over hours/days/weeks), digital insoles may have issues with device placement and sensor deterioration (Vu et al., 2020), unlike IMUs that have been shown to be comfortable and have high acceptance across various clinical populations (Keogh et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Keogh et al., 2023.

claim: Raw time-series data from digital insoles contain subject-specific latent features.
source: Nevertheless, our finding that raw time-series data contain subject-specific latent features suggests that potentially useful gait features, beyond the disease signatures studied here, may exist in this data.
evidence: This is based on the CNN analysis showing individual identification from raw time-series data.

claim: Potentially useful gait features, beyond the disease signatures studied here, may exist in raw time-series data.
source: Nevertheless, our finding that raw time-series data contain subject-specific latent features suggests that potentially useful gait features, beyond the disease signatures studied here, may exist in this data.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the finding of subject-specific features in raw data.

claim: Collecting additional timepoints from individuals may permit the model to learn more consistent subject-specific gait patterns.
source: Collecting additional timepoints from individuals may permit the model to learn more consistent subject-specific gait patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential model improvements.

claim: Individual subject gait patterns have been reported previously.
source: Individual subject gait patterns have been reported previously (Horst et al., 2019; Horst et al., 2016; Schöllhorn et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horst et al., 2019; Horst et al., 2016; Schöllhorn et al., 2002.

claim: Subject-level gait patterns and the ability to identify unique signatures of an individual's gait may enable improved monitoring of treatment responses on a per-subject as well as on a population-wide level.
source: Subject-level gait patterns and the ability to identify unique signatures of an individual's gait may enable improved monitoring of treatment responses on a per-subject as well as on a population-wide level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical applications.

claim: Training datasets with participant data from multiple visits improve the ability of the model to detect gait features that remain consistent, or that change, with time.
source: Training datasets with participant data from multiple visits improve the ability of the model to detect gait features that remain consistent, or that change, with time.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of individuality and consistency models.

claim: Collection and training on additional timepoints beyond the 2 d in our study may result in models that better learn gait features to consistently identify an individual across time.
source: Collection and training on additional timepoints beyond the 2 d in our study may result in models that better learn gait features to consistently identify an individual across time.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential model improvements with more data.

claim: By showing that vGRF data from a digital insole replicate the standard clinical data generated from force plates, we demonstrated criterion validity of vGRF data from digital insoles.
source: Holistically, by showing that vGRF data from a digital insole replicate the standard clinical data generated from force plates, we demonstrated criterion validity of vGRF data from digital insoles, meaning that digital insoles can to some degree replicate a clinical standard (the criterion).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the validation of digital insoles based on the study's findings.

claim: We demonstrated the external validity within the digital insole study of the disease gait signature across both methodologies (force plate and digital insole) using an ML approach.
source: We further demonstrated the external validity within the digital insole study of the disease gait signature across both methodologies (force plate and digital insole) using an ML approach, with a training set built entirely on force plate data and evaluated on both force plate and digital insole data collected elsewhere.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Raw sensor data lacks face value interpretability but improves upon our ability to ascertain subject-specific gait patterns.
source: Here, the fact that raw sensor data lacks face value interpretability but improves upon our ability to ascertain subject-specific gait patterns may inform us that these digital biomarker data contain disease or subject-specific information that could be leveraged in alternative clinical circumstances.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings regarding raw sensor data analysis.

claim: Digital biomarker data contain disease or subject-specific information that could be leveraged in alternative clinical circumstances.
source: Here, the fact that raw sensor data lacks face value interpretability but improves upon our ability to ascertain subject-specific gait patterns may inform us that these digital biomarker data contain disease or subject-specific information that could be leveraged in alternative clinical circumstances.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential applications of the findings.

claim: The small sample size in the pilot study of controls is a limitation of this analysis.
source: Limitations of this analysis include the small sample size in the pilot study of controls
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Subjects in the pilot study were not demographically and clinically matched with the OA study.
source: Limitations of this analysis include the small sample size in the pilot study of controls, in addition to the fact that subjects in this study were not demographically and clinically matched with the OA study.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The OA study did not control for knee-only OA on one or both joints, thus making this population heterogeneous and limiting generalizability.
source: Further, the OA study did not control for knee-only OA on one or both joints, thus making this population heterogeneous and limiting generalizability.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The study design did not specifically account for familiarization with the insoles.
source: The study design also did not specifically account for familiarization with the insoles.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The insoles are currently only capable of providing vGRF outcome measures.
source: Additionally, the insoles are currently only capable of providing vGRF outcome measures, but medial and lateral GRF would also be useful outcomes for OA as these also relate to pain and OA severity (Costello et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation, with a citation to Costello et al., 2021 supporting the utility of other GRF measures.

claim: Medial and lateral GRF would be useful outcomes for OA as these relate to pain and OA severity.
source: Additionally, the insoles are currently only capable of providing vGRF outcome measures, but medial and lateral GRF would also be useful outcomes for OA as these also relate to pain and OA severity (Costello et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Costello et al., 2021.

claim: Full analytical validation of the digital insoles was not possible as force plate and insole data was not collected simultaneously.
source: In addition, full analytical validation of the digital insoles was not possible as force plate and insole data was not collected simultaneously, and therefore evaluation of criterion and concurrent validity was not possible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Evaluation of criterion and concurrent validity was not possible because force plate and insole data was not collected simultaneously.
source: In addition, full analytical validation of the digital insoles was not possible as force plate and insole data was not collected simultaneously, and therefore evaluation of criterion and concurrent validity was not possible.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: ML approaches can help support and validate digital biomarkers and may yield digital endpoints of clinical utility.
source: This platform-agnostic analysis demonstrates that ML approaches can help support and validate digital biomarkers and may yield digital endpoints of clinical utility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Data generated from a digital insole may have unforeseen future applications such as the potential to detect changes in individual gait patterns.
source: In addition, the finding that our models can identify individual gait patterns suggests that data generated from a digital insole may have unforeseen future applications such as the potential to detect changes in individual gait patterns, which may provide better understanding of the impact of a therapeutic intervention for that individual.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about potential future applications.

claim: The GaitRec force plate vGRF dataset contained force plate control subjects (N = 211) and knee injury subjects (N = 625).
source: The GaitRec force plate vGRF dataset contained force plate control subjects (N = 211) and knee injury subjects (N = 625) (Horsak et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the dataset used, with a citation to Horsak et al., 2020.

claim: Volunteers (N = 22) were used as control subjects from a pilot study conducted between July 2019 and August 2019.
source: Volunteers were used as control subjects (N = 22) from a pilot study conducted between July 2019 and August 2019 to evaluate the usability of a digital insole to measure gait (Table 2).
evidence: This describes the pilot study participants and timing.

claim: Those pregnant or with a body mass index above 40 kg/m2 were excluded from the pilot study.
source: Those pregnant or with a body mass index above 40 kg/m2 were excluded from the study.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for the pilot study.

claim: A total of N = 44 OA patients were enrolled into a sub-study of a 259-patient clinical trial (R5069-OA-1849).
source: In the R5069-OA-1849 clinical trial, a total of N = 44 OA patients were enrolled into a sub-study of a 259-patient clinical trial.
evidence: This describes the clinical trial sub-study enrollment.

claim: Each Moticon digital insole has a total of 25 sensors per foot: 16 vertical plantar pressure sensors that assess force, a trial-axial accelerometer that measures acceleration, and a gyroscope that measures orientation and angular velocity.
source: Each Moticon digital insole has a total of 25 sensors per foot: 16 vertical plantar pressure sensors that assess force, a trial-axial accelerometer that measures acceleration, and a gyroscope that measures orientation and angular velocity.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the Moticon digital insole.

claim: Each sensor in the Moticon digital insole captures data at 100Hz.
source: Each sensor captures data at 100Hz, and dedicated software computes several clinically relevant spatial and temporal-derived gait characteristics comparable to data generated in a gait lab.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the Moticon digital insole.

claim: The Moticon digital insole computes vGRF in the same way as a force plate, generating comparable data outputs.
source: The Moticon digital insole computes vGRF in the same way as a force plate, generating comparable data outputs.
evidence: This describes the measurement approach of the Moticon digital insole.
